title: CISA Manual · Study Guide
edition: Follows the structure of the CISA Review Manual, 28th edition: every section and numbered subsection. Original study notes, not the manual text.

sections.title: IS Audit Standards, Guidelines, Functions and Codes of Ethics
sections.summary: Sets the professional rules every IS auditor works under: ISACA’s IT Audit Framework (ITAF), the Code of Professional Ethics, and how the audit function is organised and given authority through a charter.
points: ITAF standards are mandatory; guidelines explain how to apply them; tools and techniques give practical examples.
Standards are grouped as general (independence, objectivity, proficiency, due care), performance (planning, risk assessment, evidence, using the work of others) and reporting.
The audit charter defines purpose, authority, responsibility and accountability, and is approved by the board or audit committee.
Internal audit reports functionally to the audit committee and administratively to senior management to protect independence.
The Code of Professional Ethics requires due care, objectivity, confidentiality, competence and support for standards; breaches can lead to disciplinary action.

terms.d: ISACA’s IT Audit Framework: the set of mandatory standards plus supporting guidelines and techniques.
Formal document that establishes the audit function’s mandate and unrestricted access.
Being free of relationships that a reasonable third party would see as compromising objectivity.

auditor: Confirm the charter exists, is approved at board level and is reviewed periodically.
Check reporting lines and whether auditors have assessed and disclosed any impairment.
traps: The auditor never approves or implements controls; doing so impairs independence.
When independence is impaired, disclose it; do not simply continue.

subs.title: ISACA IS Audit and Assurance Standards
points: Mandatory requirements for anyone performing IS audit and assurance work under ISACA.
Grouped as general, performance and reporting standards.
Non-compliance must be justified and disclosed.
subs.tip: Standards = must; guidelines = should.

subs.title: ISACA IS Audit and Assurance Guidelines
points: Explain how to apply the standards in practice.
Not mandatory, but departures should be justifiable.

subs.title: ISACA Code of Professional Ethics
points: Members support standards, act with objectivity and due care, keep information confidential and maintain competence.
Members inform stakeholders of results and support professional education.
Failure to comply can lead to investigation and disciplinary measures.
subs.tip: Confidentiality applies unless disclosure is legally required.

subs.title: ITAF
points: IT Audit Framework: ISACA’s overall framework of standards, guidelines and tools and techniques.
Defines roles, responsibilities, knowledge and skills expected of IS auditors.

subs.title: IS Internal Audit Function
points: Established by an approved audit charter; independent of the areas it audits.
Audit committee oversees the plan, resources and results.
May include an audit plan based on risk and stakeholder needs.
subs.tip: The charter, not the engagement letter, grants overall authority to internal audit.

sections.title: Types of Audits, Assessments and Reviews
sections.summary: Explains the different engagements an IS auditor may perform and how audits differ from assessments and reviews, including reliance on third-party assurance reports.
points: Audit types include compliance, financial, operational, integrated, administrative, IS, specialised and forensic audits.
An integrated audit combines financial, operational and IS audit work to assess controls across a business process.
Assessments (e.g. risk or control self-assessments) are often less formal and may be performed by management.
Third-party service audits (e.g. SOC 1 / SOC 2 reports) let user organisations rely on a provider’s controls; check report type, period and exceptions.
Forensic audits collect evidence for possible legal action and must protect chain of custody.

terms.d: Type 1 covers control design at a point in time; Type 2 also tests operating effectiveness over a period.
A single engagement covering financial, operational and IT controls together.

auditor: When relying on another auditor’s report, evaluate their independence, competence, scope and period covered.
Review complementary user entity controls the client must operate.
traps: A Type 1 report gives no assurance that controls worked over time.
A SOC report outside your audit period needs bridge letters or extra testing.

subs.title: Control Self-Assessment
points: Management and staff assess controls, often in facilitated workshops.
Benefits: earlier detection of risk, ownership of controls, improved awareness, reduced audit cost.
Disadvantages: may be mistaken for an audit replacement; workshop scheduling; reliance on participants’ objectivity.
The IS auditor acts as facilitator and still provides independent assurance.
subs.tip: CSA objective: shift responsibility for control monitoring to the business.

subs.title: Integrated Auditing
points: Combines financial, operational and IS audit work to assess the internal control of a business process.
Key steps: identify risk and key controls, review and understand design, test and assess, report.
Gives a holistic view and avoids duplicated testing.

sections.title: Risk-Based Audit Planning
sections.summary: Shows how auditors plan engagements and the annual plan around risk, so effort goes where the organisation is most exposed.
points: Start by understanding business objectives, processes, IT environment and applicable laws and regulations.
Audit risk = inherent risk × control risk × detection risk; auditors manage detection risk through the nature, timing and extent of testing.
Risk-based planning prioritises high-risk areas and documents why areas are in or out of scope.
Materiality in IS audit considers both monetary amount and non-monetary impact (e.g. safety, reputation, regulatory breach).
Risk assessment techniques range from qualitative scoring to quantitative models; results drive the audit plan and resource allocation.

terms.d: Risk before any controls are considered.
Risk that controls will not prevent or detect a material error.
Risk that audit procedures will not detect a material error.

auditor: Revisit the risk assessment when significant change occurs (new systems, incidents, regulations).
Link each audit objective to a specific risk.
traps: The auditor cannot change inherent or control risk, only detection risk.
The first step in planning is understanding the business, not choosing tests.

subs.title: Individual Audit Assignments
points: Each engagement is planned considering objectives, prior audit results, risk and resources.
Understand the business process, systems, interfaces and control environment.

subs.title: Effect of Laws and Regulations on IS Audit Planning
points: Identify legal and regulatory requirements relevant to the area (e.g. privacy, financial reporting).
Determine whether management has processes to comply and monitor compliance.
Regulations can set scope, frequency and evidence requirements.
subs.tip: Step 1: identify external requirements; then check management’s compliance process.

subs.title: Audit Risk and Materiality
points: Audit risk = inherent × control × detection risk.
Materiality considers monetary and non-monetary impact (e.g. regulatory, reputational, safety).
In IS audit, a small control weakness can be material if it affects many transactions or critical systems.

subs.title: Risk Assessment
points: Identify assets, threats and vulnerabilities; evaluate likelihood and impact.
Prioritise audit areas by risk.
Repeat periodically and after major changes.

subs.title: IS Audit Risk Assessment Techniques
points: Scoring systems, judgement-based ranking, and quantitative models.
Combines business impact, control environment and prior findings.
Documented so prioritisation can be explained.

subs.title: Risk Analysis
points: Analyses events that could prevent objectives being met.
Supports planning, focusing tests on key risks and controls.

sections.title: Types of Controls and Considerations
sections.summary: Describes control classifications, control objectives and how general and application controls work together.
points: Controls are preventive, detective or corrective; also deterrent, compensating and recovery in some models.
Control objectives state what a control must achieve (e.g. only authorised changes reach production).
IT general controls (access, change, operations, backup) support the reliability of application controls.
Application controls cover input, processing and output; automated controls are tested once if ITGCs are effective.
Compensating controls reduce risk when a primary control (e.g. segregation of duties) cannot be applied.

terms.d: An alternative control that reduces the risk left by a missing or weak primary control.
IT general controls over the environment in which applications run.

auditor: Test ITGCs before relying on automated application controls.
Assess control design first, then operating effectiveness.
traps: Preventive controls are generally preferred, but the BEST answer depends on the risk described.
Review of logs is detective, not preventive.

subs.title: Internal Controls
points: Policies, procedures, practices and structures that give reasonable assurance objectives are met.
Address both preventing and detecting undesired events.
subs.tip: Controls give reasonable, not absolute, assurance.

subs.title: Control Objectives and Control Measures
points: A control objective states the result a control must achieve.
Control measures are the specific activities implementing the objective.
IS control objectives include safeguarding assets, data integrity, reliability, efficiency and compliance.

subs.title: Control Classifications
points: Preventive, detective, corrective (also deterrent, compensating, recovery).
Manual vs automated; general vs application controls.

subs.title: Control Relationship to Risk
points: Controls are selected to reduce specific risks to an acceptable level.
Cost of a control should not exceed the benefit of risk reduction.

subs.title: Prescriptive Controls and Frameworks
points: Frameworks such as COBIT, ISO/IEC 27002 and NIST give control catalogues.
Prescriptive controls may be required by regulation or contract.

subs.title: Evaluation of the Control Environment
points: Assess tone at the top, organisation, policies, risk management and monitoring.
A weak control environment reduces reliance on individual controls.

sections.title: Audit Project Management
sections.summary: Covers running an audit as a project: objectives, scope, work program, resources, schedule, supervision and communication.
points: Define audit objectives and scope, then design the audit program (procedures to collect evidence).
Plan resources and skills; use specialists where needed and supervise their work.
Agree timing and logistics with auditee management; hold an opening meeting.
Monitor progress, document work papers and review them before conclusions are drawn.

terms.d: The step-by-step procedures to achieve audit objectives.
Documented evidence of planning, procedures, results and conclusions.

auditor: Check work papers support every finding and are reviewed by a senior auditor.
traps: Scope changes requested by the auditee must be assessed for independence impact and documented.

subs.title: Audit Objectives
points: Specific goals of the audit, e.g. confirm that access controls prevent unauthorised changes.
Drive scope, procedures and evidence.

subs.title: Audit Phases
points: Planning: subject, objective, scope, pre-audit planning, data gathering procedures.
Fieldwork: acquire data, test controls, issue discovery and validation.
Reporting/follow-up: report, exit meeting, follow-up on actions.

subs.title: Audit Programs
points: Step-by-step procedures and instructions to achieve the audit objectives.
Used for consistency and supervision; adapted to the specific environment.

subs.title: Audit Work Papers
points: Document planning, procedures performed, evidence and conclusions.
Must be retained, protected and reviewed.
subs.tip: If it is not documented, it was not done.

subs.title: Fraud, Irregularities and Illegal Acts
points: Management is primarily responsible for preventing and detecting fraud.
The auditor considers fraud risk in planning and reports indicators to the appropriate level.
Auditors do not guarantee fraud detection.
subs.tip: If fraud is suspected, report to appropriate management or the audit committee, not to the suspects.

subs.title: Agile Auditing
points: Iterative, sprint-based audit work with frequent stakeholder communication.
Prioritised backlog of audit tasks; quicker delivery of insights.
Standards and evidence requirements still apply.

sections.title: Audit Testing and Sampling Methodology
sections.summary: Explains compliance versus substantive testing and how to use statistical and non-statistical sampling.
points: Compliance tests check whether controls operate as designed; substantive tests check the accuracy of data and balances.
Attribute sampling estimates rates (used for compliance testing); variable sampling estimates amounts (substantive).
Stop-or-go sampling stops early when few errors are expected; discovery sampling checks for at least one occurrence (e.g. fraud).
Sample size rises with confidence level and expected error rate, and falls as tolerable error rises.
Statistical sampling allows the risk of sampling error to be quantified; judgmental sampling does not.

terms.d: Maximum error rate or amount the auditor will accept and still conclude a control is effective.
Probability that the sample results represent the population.
Dividing a population into groups with similar characteristics to improve sampling efficiency.

auditor: Choose sampling based on the test objective; document the method so results can be defended.
traps: When controls are weak, increase substantive testing rather than relying on compliance tests.
Use statistical sampling when an objective, defensible conclusion is needed.

subs.title: Compliance Versus Substantive Testing
points: Compliance tests: do controls operate as designed?
Substantive tests: is the data/transaction accurate and complete?
Results of compliance testing determine the extent of substantive testing.

subs.title: Sampling
points: Statistical (attribute, variable, stop-or-go, discovery) vs non-statistical sampling.
Key terms: confidence coefficient, precision, expected error rate, tolerable error, population standard deviation.
Stratification and representative selection improve efficiency.
subs.tip: Higher confidence → bigger sample; bigger tolerable error → smaller sample.

sections.title: Audit Evidence Collection Techniques
sections.summary: Describes what makes evidence sufficient and reliable and the techniques used to gather it.
points: Evidence must be sufficient, reliable, relevant and useful to support conclusions.
Reliability is higher for independent sources, evidence obtained directly by the auditor, and objective system data.
Techniques: inquiry, observation, inspection of documents, reperformance, analytical procedures, CAATs, interviews and walk-throughs.
Preserve and protect evidence; maintain chain of custody when legal action is possible.

terms.d: The auditor independently executes a control or calculation to verify results.
Documented, unbroken record of who handled evidence and when.

auditor: Corroborate verbal evidence with documents or system data.
traps: Evidence from the auditee is less reliable than evidence the auditor obtains directly.
Observation is reliable only for the moment it occurred.

subs.title: Interviewing and Observing Personnel in Performance of Their Duties
points: Observation and interviews show how processes really work.
Corroborate with documents and data; observation only proves what was seen at that moment.

sections.title: Audit Data Analytics
sections.summary: Shows how data analytics, CAATs and continuous auditing extend coverage and find anomalies across whole populations.
points: CAATs and generalised audit software test 100% of transactions to find duplicates, gaps, outliers and exceptions.
Continuous auditing techniques: embedded audit modules (SCARF), integrated test facility, snapshots, audit hooks, continuous and intermittent simulation.
Data must be extracted completely and accurately; validate record counts and totals before analysis.
Analytics also support risk assessment and fraud detection; algorithms must be documented and tested.

terms.d: Integrated test facility: fictitious entity processed alongside live data.
Assurance provided simultaneously with, or shortly after, the events it covers.

auditor: Confirm data integrity and access controls over the audit data copy.
traps: ITF test data must be reversed so it does not affect real results.
Continuous auditing suits high-volume automated environments.

subs.title: Computer-Assisted Audit Techniques
points: Generalised audit software, utilities, test data, application tracing and mapping.
Allow full-population testing and independent recalculation.
Plan data access, extraction integrity and confidentiality.

subs.title: Continuous Auditing and Monitoring
points: Continuous monitoring is management’s responsibility; continuous auditing gives independent assurance.
Suited to paperless, high-volume, automated environments.

subs.title: Continuous Auditing Techniques
points: SCARF/EAM, integrated test facility, snapshots, audit hooks, continuous and intermittent simulation.
Choice depends on complexity and timing needs.
subs.tip: Audit hooks: low complexity, flag selected transactions for review.

subs.title: Artificial Intelligence in IS Audit
points: AI can analyse large data sets, detect anomalies and support risk assessment.
Auditors must understand model limits, bias, data quality and explainability.
Professional judgement remains with the auditor.

sections.title: Reporting and Communication Techniques
sections.summary: Covers communicating results: exit meetings, report structure, rating findings and follow-up.
points: Discuss findings with auditee management before issuing the report to confirm facts.
Report findings with condition, criteria, cause, effect and recommendation, plus management’s response.
Rate findings by risk so priorities are clear; summarise for senior management and the audit committee.
Follow up to verify that agreed actions were implemented; escalate overdue high-risk items.

terms.d: Meeting to discuss findings and agree facts before the final report.
Process to confirm that corrective actions were implemented and effective.

auditor: Make sure every recommendation addresses the root cause, not just the symptom.
traps: The auditor must not drop a valid finding because management disagrees; report it with management’s view.

subs.title: Communicating Audit Results
points: Exit interview to confirm facts and agree recommendations and dates.
Communication is ongoing, not only at the end.

subs.title: Audit Report Objectives
points: Give an opinion on control adequacy, report findings and recommendations, and enable action.

subs.title: Audit Report Structure and Contents
points: Introduction (scope, objectives, period), overall conclusion/opinion, detailed findings and recommendations, management responses, limitations.
Findings rated by risk.

subs.title: Audit Documentation
points: Supports the report; shows planning, evidence, review and conclusions.
Retention and access follow policy and law.

subs.title: Follow-Up Activities
points: Verify agreed actions are implemented and effective.
Escalate overdue or ineffective actions.

subs.title: Types of IS Audit Reports
points: Internal audit reports, assurance reports for third parties (e.g. SOC), regulatory and special-purpose reports.

sections.title: Quality Assurance and Improvement of the Audit Process
sections.summary: Explains how the audit function assures its own quality through internal and external quality reviews and control self-assessment.
points: A quality assurance and improvement program includes ongoing supervision, periodic internal assessments and external reviews.
Control self-assessment (CSA) workshops let management and staff evaluate their own controls; auditors facilitate.
Audit methodology, training and tools should be updated as risks and technology change.

terms.d: Control self-assessment: management-led evaluation of controls, often in facilitated workshops.

auditor: Check that lessons learned from reviews are fed back into the audit methodology.
traps: CSA supplements internal audit; it does not replace it.

subs.title: Audit Committee Oversight
points: Approves charter and plan, reviews results and monitors independence and resources.

subs.title: Audit Quality Assurance
points: Supervision, internal reviews and periodic external assessments of the audit function.

subs.title: Audit Team Training and Development
points: Continuing education to keep skills current with technology and risk.

subs.title: Monitoring
points: Track audit performance metrics and feed improvements into methodology.

sections.title: Laws, Regulations and Industry Standards
sections.summary: How external obligations (laws, regulations, contracts and industry standards) shape IT governance and what the auditor checks.
points: Management must identify all applicable legal, regulatory and contractual requirements and assign owners.
Requirements are translated into policies and controls and monitored for ongoing compliance.
Industry standards (ISO/IEC 27001, PCI DSS, NIST) may be mandatory by contract or adopted voluntarily.
Changes in laws must trigger review of policies, controls and contracts.

terms.d: Conforming with laws, regulations, contracts and internal policies.

auditor: Check there is a register of obligations with owners and evidence of monitoring.
traps: The first step is identifying which requirements apply, before testing compliance.

sections.title: Organizational Structure, IT Governance and IT Strategy
sections.summary: Explains governance of enterprise IT (GEIT), governance structures and committees, and how IT strategy is aligned to business strategy.
points: Governance (board) evaluates, directs and monitors; management plans, builds, runs and monitors (COBIT 2019).
IT strategy committee (board level) advises on strategic alignment; IT steering committee (executive level) prioritises and oversees projects and investments.
IT strategy must derive from business strategy and be approved by senior management.
Organisational structure must support segregation of duties between development, operations, security and users.
Good practice frameworks: COBIT 2019, ISO/IEC 38500, ITIL; balanced scorecard for performance.

terms.d: Governance of enterprise IT: ensuring IT creates value, manages risk and uses resources in line with business goals.
Splitting incompatible duties so no single person can both commit and conceal an error or fraud.

auditor: Review committee charters, minutes and evidence that IT strategy is reviewed against business plans.
Check SoD conflicts in IT roles (e.g. developer with production access).
traps: Board-level oversight is the strategy committee; project prioritisation is the steering committee.
Strategy alignment is the PRIMARY objective of IT governance.

subs.title: Enterprise Governance of Information and Technology
points: EGIT ensures I&T supports strategy, delivers value and manages risk and resources.
Board-level responsibility within corporate governance.

subs.title: Good Practices for EGIT
points: Use frameworks such as COBIT 2019 and ISO/IEC 38500.
Clear decision rights, accountability, performance measures.

subs.title: Audit’s Role in EGIT
points: Evaluate alignment, governance structures, risk management and performance measurement.
Report to the board/audit committee.

subs.title: Information Security Governance
points: Board and executives set security direction, risk appetite and accountability.
Security strategy is aligned with business objectives.
subs.tip: Senior management commitment is the key success factor.

subs.title: Information Systems Strategy
points: Long-term plan for using IS to support business goals.
Approved and reviewed by senior management.

subs.title: Strategic Planning
points: Translates business strategy into IT initiatives, roadmaps and budgets.

subs.title: Business Intelligence
points: Collecting and analysing data for decisions; requires data governance and quality controls.
Risks: inconsistent definitions, poor data quality, unauthorised access.

subs.title: Organizational Structure
points: Roles: board, IT strategy committee, steering committee, CIO/CISO, data owners, custodians.
Segregation of duties across development, operations, security and users.
Compensating controls when SoD is not possible.

subs.title: Auditing IT Governance Structure and Implementation
points: Review documents (strategy, policies, minutes), reporting lines and SoD.
Indicators of problems: misalignment, lack of sponsorship, excessive costs, frequent failures.

sections.title: IT Policies, Standards, Procedures and Guidelines
sections.summary: Describes the policy hierarchy and how policies are developed, approved, communicated and reviewed.
points: Policies state management intent and are approved by senior management/board; standards are mandatory specifics; procedures give steps; guidelines are advisory.
Policies must be communicated, acknowledged and periodically reviewed.
Lower-level policies must align with the enterprise information security policy.
Exceptions must be documented, risk-assessed and approved.

terms.d: Mandatory requirement that supports a policy (e.g. password length).
Recommended, non-mandatory practice.

auditor: Compare policies with regulations and good practice; test that procedures are followed in practice.
traps: An unapproved or outdated policy is a governance weakness even if staff follow it.

subs.title: Policies
points: High-level statements of management intent; approved by senior management.
Reviewed periodically and communicated to all staff.

subs.title: Standards
points: Mandatory rules that support policies.

subs.title: Procedures
points: Detailed steps to implement policies and standards.

subs.title: Guidelines
points: Recommended practices; not mandatory.

sections.title: Enterprise Architecture and Considerations
sections.summary: Explains enterprise architecture (EA) as the blueprint linking business, data, applications and technology.
points: EA documents current and target states and the roadmap between them.
Frameworks include Zachman and TOGAF; layers cover business, data, application and technology.
EA reduces duplication, supports standardisation and informs investment decisions.

terms.d: Structured description of how business processes, information and technology fit together.

auditor: Check projects are reviewed for compliance with the target architecture.
traps: EA is a planning and governance tool, not a technical diagram only.

sections.title: Enterprise Risk Management
sections.summary: Covers building a risk management program: context, identification, analysis, treatment, monitoring and reporting.
points: A risk management program needs objectives, scope, roles, risk appetite and reporting set by senior management.
Process: identify assets, threats and vulnerabilities; assess likelihood and impact; treat; monitor and communicate.
Treatment options: mitigate, transfer/share, avoid, accept within appetite.
Risk registers track owners, ratings, treatments and residual risk; risk is reassessed after significant change.

terms.d: The amount of risk an organisation is willing to accept in pursuit of its objectives.
Risk remaining after treatment.

auditor: Check risks are linked to business objectives and that acceptance is signed off by authorised owners.
traps: Risk acceptance is a management decision, never the auditor’s.

subs.title: Developing a Risk Management Program
points: Establish purpose, scope, responsibilities, risk appetite and documentation.
Gain senior management commitment and resources.

subs.title: Risk Management Life Cycle
points: Identify assets, evaluate threats and vulnerabilities, assess impact, calculate risk, treat, monitor.
Risk treatment: mitigate, transfer, avoid, accept.

subs.title: Risk Analysis Methods
points: Qualitative (high/medium/low), semi-quantitative (scored scales) and quantitative (monetary values, e.g. ALE).
subs.tip: ALE = single loss expectancy × annual rate of occurrence.

sections.title: Data Privacy Program and Principles
sections.summary: Explains how organisations manage personal data across its lifecycle and comply with privacy laws.
points: Privacy principles: lawfulness, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security, accountability, individual rights.
Privacy impact assessments (PIAs/DPIAs) identify privacy risk early in new systems or changes.
Roles include data protection officer and data owners; third parties processing data need contracts.
Breach notification requirements must be built into incident response.

terms.d: Privacy impact assessment: structured review of privacy risk in a process or system.

auditor: Check data inventories, consent records, retention schedules and PIA evidence.
traps: Privacy (rights over personal data) is not the same as confidentiality (protection from disclosure).

subs.title: Privacy Documentation
points: Privacy notices, records of processing, data inventories, PIAs and policies.

subs.title: Audit Process
points: Assess compliance with privacy laws and policies across the data lifecycle.

sections.title: Data Governance and Classification
sections.summary: Covers managing data as an asset: ownership, quality, lifecycle and classification.
points: Data owners classify data by sensitivity and criticality and approve access.
Classification drives handling, encryption, retention and disposal requirements.
Data quality dimensions include accuracy, completeness, consistency and timeliness.
Data lifecycle: create, store, use, share, archive, destroy.

terms.d: Business person accountable for a data set’s classification and access.
IT role that implements the owner’s requirements.

auditor: Test that classification labels are applied and controls match the class.
traps: Classification is the owner’s responsibility, not IT’s.

subs.title: Data Inventory and Classification
points: Know what data you hold, where it is and how sensitive it is.

subs.title: Legal Purpose, Consent and Legitimate Interest
points: Processing personal data needs a lawful basis such as consent or legitimate interest.

subs.title: Data Subject Rights
points: Rights to access, correct, delete, restrict and port data; processes must meet legal deadlines.

sections.title: IT Resource Management
sections.summary: Covers managing IT people, budgets, investments and assets for value.
points: IT investment decisions use business cases and portfolio management.
HR practices: hiring checks, training, job rotation, mandatory leave, termination procedures.
Financial management: budgeting, cost allocation/chargeback, tracking benefits.

terms.d: Charging IT costs to the business units that consume services.

auditor: Check key-person dependencies, training plans and termination access removal.
traps: Mandatory leave and rotation are detective controls for fraud.

subs.title: Value of IT
points: IT investments must deliver measurable business value.

subs.title: Implementing IT Portfolio Management
points: Manage IT investments as a portfolio; prioritise by value and risk.

subs.title: IT Management Practices
points: Policies, processes and controls for planning, delivering and supporting IT.

subs.title: Human Resource Management
points: Hiring, background checks, training, performance, rotation, mandatory leave, termination.
subs.tip: Terminated users’ access must be removed immediately.

subs.title: Enterprise Change Management
points: Managing organisational change so people adopt new processes and systems.

subs.title: Financial Management Practices
points: Budgeting, cost allocation, chargeback and tracking IT spend.

subs.title: Information Security Management
points: Ongoing management of security programme, aligned with governance.

sections.title: IT Vendor Management
sections.summary: Explains sourcing strategies and managing third parties across the contract lifecycle.
points: Sourcing options: insourcing, outsourcing, cloud, onshore/offshore, hybrid.
Due diligence before selection; contracts with SLAs, security, right-to-audit, data ownership, exit and subcontracting clauses.
Ongoing monitoring of performance and risk; independent assurance reports (e.g. SOC 2).
Accountability for risk remains with the organisation.

terms.d: Contract term allowing the customer or its auditors to audit the vendor.

auditor: Review vendor risk assessments, SLA reports and how exceptions are followed up.
traps: Outsourcing transfers the activity, not the accountability.

subs.title: Sourcing Practices
points: Insourced, outsourced, hybrid; onsite, offsite, offshore.

subs.title: Outsourcing Practices and Strategies
points: Due diligence, contract terms, SLAs, right to audit, exit plans.

subs.title: Cloud Governance
points: Policies for selecting, using and monitoring cloud services; shared responsibility.

subs.title: Governance in Outsourcing
points: Accountability stays with the organisation; monitor the provider.

subs.title: Capacity and Growth Planning
points: Plan for vendor capacity and scalability as the business grows.

subs.title: Third-Party Service Delivery Management
points: Monitor performance, review reports, manage changes and incidents with vendors.

sections.title: IT Performance Monitoring and Reporting
sections.summary: Covers measuring IT performance with KPIs, KRIs and balanced scorecards and reporting to governance bodies.
points: KPIs measure performance; KRIs give early warning of rising risk.
The IT balanced scorecard links IT measures to business goals across several perspectives.
Maturity/capability models assess process improvement.
Metrics must be relevant, reliable and reported to the right audience.

terms.d: Key risk indicator: metric signalling increased risk exposure.

auditor: Test the accuracy of reported metrics back to source data.
traps: Metrics that are not aligned to business objectives have little governance value.

subs.title: Key Performance Indicators
points: Measure how well processes achieve goals.

subs.title: Key Risk Indicators
points: Early warning metrics of increasing risk exposure.

subs.title: Key Control Indicators
points: Measure how well controls are operating.

subs.title: Performance Optimization
points: Continuous improvement of IT processes and resources.

subs.title: Approaches and Techniques
points: Balanced scorecard, benchmarking, maturity models, Six Sigma, Lean.

sections.title: Quality Assurance and Quality Management of IT
sections.summary: Explains quality management systems and QA for IT processes and products.
points: QA checks adherence to processes and standards; quality control tests products.
ISO 9001 quality management; continuous improvement (plan-do-check-act).
QA should be independent of the teams it reviews.

terms.d: Activities that ensure processes are followed to produce quality outcomes.

auditor: Check QA reviews happen, are independent and lead to corrective action.
traps: QA is process-focused; QC is product-focused.

subs.title: Quality Assurance
points: Independent checking that processes follow standards.

subs.title: Quality Management
points: Systems such as ISO 9001; plan-do-check-act.

subs.title: Operational Excellence
points: Consistently efficient, reliable operations through standardisation and improvement.

chapters.title: Information Systems Acquisition, Development and Implementation

sections.title: Project Governance and Management
sections.summary: Covers portfolio, program and project management, project roles, planning techniques and project control.
points: Portfolio management selects and balances projects against strategy; programs group related projects.
Roles: sponsor (funding, accountability), steering committee (direction), project manager (delivery), users (requirements, acceptance), QA, security.
Planning tools: WBS, Gantt, critical path method, PERT, function point analysis, earned value.
Control scope with formal change requests; track time, cost and quality; manage project risk.
Close projects formally: acceptance, lessons learned, documentation handover.

terms.d: Longest sequence of dependent tasks; any delay delays the project.
Compares planned value, earned value and actual cost to measure progress.
Estimates software size from its functions (inputs, outputs, files, interfaces, inquiries).

auditor: Check governance gates, status reporting accuracy and change control over scope.
traps: Project sponsor owns the business case.
Scope creep without change control is a key risk.

subs.title: Project Management Practices
points: Apply structured methods (e.g. PMBOK, PRINCE2) to deliver on time, budget and quality.

subs.title: Project Management Structure
points: Functional, project-based (pure) and matrix organisations; authority of the project manager differs.

subs.title: Project Management Roles and Responsibilities
points: Sponsor, steering committee, project manager, user management, system development management, QA, security officer.
subs.tip: The sponsor owns the business case and funding.

subs.title: Project Management Techniques
points: WBS, Gantt charts, CPM, PERT, timeboxing, function point analysis, earned value.

subs.title: Portfolio/Program Management
points: Portfolio optimises the set of projects; programmes coordinate related projects toward a shared outcome.

subs.title: Project Management Office
points: Supports projects with standards, tools, reporting and governance.

subs.title: Project Benefits Realization
points: Define, track and measure benefits from approval to after go-live.

subs.title: Project Initiation
points: Charter, sponsor, objectives and approval to start.

subs.title: Project Objectives
points: Specific, measurable outcomes; often broken into a WBS and work packages.

subs.title: Project Planning
points: Estimate effort, schedule, budget and resources; identify risks.

subs.title: Project Execution
points: Coordinate people and resources to carry out the plan.

subs.title: Project Controlling and Monitoring
points: Track progress, manage scope changes, resources and risks.
subs.tip: Uncontrolled scope change is a key failure cause.

subs.title: Project Closing
points: Formal acceptance, lessons learned, handover, release of resources.

subs.title: IS Auditor’s Role in Project Management
points: Review governance, controls and risks during the project; advise without taking ownership.

sections.title: Business Case and Feasibility Analysis
sections.summary: Explains justifying investments and assessing technical, economic and operational feasibility.
points: The business case states the problem, options, costs, benefits, risks and alignment with strategy.
Feasibility covers technical, economic (ROI, NPV, payback), operational, legal and schedule factors.
The business case is revisited at phase gates; benefits are tracked after implementation.

terms.d: Return on investment: benefit relative to cost.

auditor: Check the business case was approved and updated when assumptions changed.
traps: A project that no longer meets its business case should be re-evaluated or stopped.

subs.title: IS Auditor’s Role in Business Case Development
points: Check the business case is complete, realistic and approved, and benefits are measurable.

sections.title: System Development Methodologies
sections.summary: Compares SDLC approaches and acquisition options, and what controls each needs.
points: Waterfall: sequential phases with sign-offs; suits stable requirements.
Agile (e.g. Scrum): short iterations, user collaboration, working software; controls must be built into the process.
Other approaches: prototyping, RAD, DevOps/DevSecOps, object-oriented and component-based development, reverse/re-engineering.
Buying software: requirements, RFP, vendor evaluation, contract, escrow for source code.

terms.d: Third party holds vendor source code, released if the vendor fails.
Integrating security into automated development and operations pipelines.

auditor: Check requirements traceability, user involvement and security requirements in every approach.
traps: Lack of user involvement in requirements is a leading cause of failure.

subs.title: Business Application Development
points: Building or acquiring applications to meet business requirements with controls built in.

subs.title: SDLC Models
points: Waterfall, V-model, iterative/incremental, spiral and agile.

subs.title: SDLC Phases
points: Feasibility, requirements, design, development, testing, implementation, post-implementation.
Each phase ends with deliverables and approval.

subs.title: IS Auditor’s Role in SDLC Project Management
points: Review controls at each phase: requirements, security, testing, change control, sign-offs.

subs.title: Software Development Methods
points: Agile, prototyping, RAD, object-oriented, component-based, DevOps, reverse engineering.

subs.title: System Development Tools and Productivity Aids
points: CASE tools, code generators, low-code platforms; need controls over generated code.

subs.title: Infrastructure Development/Acquisition Practices
points: Plan infrastructure requirements, capacity and security before acquisition.

subs.title: Hardware/Software Acquisition
points: Requirements, invitation to tender/RFP, vendor evaluation, contract, acceptance testing.

subs.title: System Software Acquisition
points: Evaluate compatibility, security, support and licensing of operating systems and utilities.

sections.title: Control Identification and Design
sections.summary: Covers designing application controls: input, processing, output and data integrity.
points: Input controls: validation edits (sequence, limit, range, validity, reasonableness, check digit, completeness, duplicate, logical relationship).
Processing controls: run-to-run totals, reconciliation, edit checks on calculations, exception reports.
Output controls: distribution, balancing, secure handling and retention.
Data integrity: ACID properties, referential and relational integrity.

terms.d: Calculated digit appended to a number to detect transcription errors.
A transaction either completes fully or not at all.

auditor: Confirm controls are designed during development, not added after go-live.
traps: Hash totals detect missing or altered records; they have no business meaning.

subs.title: Application Controls
points: Input/origination, processing, and data file controls; batch controls and validation edits.

subs.title: Output Controls
points: Logging and storage of sensitive forms, distribution, balancing and reconciliation, retention.

sections.title: System Readiness and Implementation Testing
sections.summary: Explains testing levels and approaches before go-live.
points: Unit, integration/interface, system, acceptance (UAT and QAT) testing.
System testing includes recovery, security, load, volume, stress and performance testing.
Regression testing confirms changes did not break existing functions; parallel testing compares old and new systems.
Test data should be representative and protected; production data used in testing must be masked.

terms.d: User acceptance testing: users confirm the system meets business requirements.
Re-running tests to make sure changes did not introduce errors.

auditor: Check test plans, results, defect resolution and formal user sign-off.
traps: Users, not IT, sign off acceptance testing.

subs.title: Testing Classifications
points: Unit, interface, system, final acceptance testing.

subs.title: Software Testing
points: Top-down vs bottom-up; white-box and black-box.

subs.title: Data Integrity Testing
points: Relational and referential integrity tests; ACID properties.

subs.title: Application Systems Testing
points: Snapshots, mapping, tracing, test data, ITF, parallel simulation.

subs.title: System Implementation
points: Plan go-live, train users, prepare support and fallback.

sections.title: Implementation Configuration and Release Management
sections.summary: Covers configuration baselines and controlled release into production.
points: Configuration management maintains approved baselines and versions (e.g. CMDB).
Releases are planned, tested, approved, scheduled and include rollback plans.
Migration to production is done by a function independent of developers.

terms.d: Approved configuration used as a reference for future changes.

auditor: Test that what is in production matches the approved release.
traps: Developers moving their own code to production breaks segregation of duties.

subs.title: Configuration Management Systems
points: Track versions and baselines of configuration items; prevent unauthorised change.

sections.title: System Migration, Infrastructure Deployment and Data Conversion
sections.summary: Explains changeover methods and controls over migrating data and infrastructure.
points: Changeover: parallel (safest), phased, pilot, abrupt/direct (riskiest).
Data conversion controls: record counts, control totals, reconciliation, error reports, user sign-off.
Fallback plans and backups are required before cutover.

terms.d: Running old and new systems together until the new one is proven.

auditor: Verify reconciliation of converted data and approval of exceptions.
traps: Data conversion without reconciliation is a major risk to data integrity.

subs.title: Data Migration
points: Plan, extract, cleanse, convert, load and reconcile data.
Controls: record counts, control totals, exception reports, sign-off.

subs.title: Changeover (Go-Live or Cutover) Techniques
points: Parallel, phased, abrupt changeover; each needs a fallback plan.

subs.title: System Change Procedures and the Program Migration Process
points: Changes follow approval and testing; migration to production done by an independent function.

subs.title: System Software Implementation
points: Install and configure system software with testing and change control.

subs.title: Certification/Accreditation
points: Certification: technical evaluation of controls. Accreditation: management accepts residual risk.

sections.title: Postimplementation Review
sections.summary: Covers evaluating whether a project achieved its objectives and benefits after go-live.
points: PIR assesses benefits realisation, user satisfaction, controls and lessons learned.
Performed once the system has stabilised; independence of reviewers matters.
Results feed future projects and the portfolio process.

terms.d: Postimplementation review.

auditor: Compare actual results with the business case.
traps: A PIR too soon after go-live gives an incomplete picture.

subs.title: IS Auditor’s Role in Postimplementation Review
points: Assess benefits, controls and lessons; ideally by someone not involved in the project.

chapters.title: Information Systems Operations and Business Resilience

sections.title: IT Components
sections.summary: Introduces the hardware, software, network and cloud components an auditor must understand and their key risks.
points: Hardware: servers, storage, end-user devices; operating systems and middleware.
Networks: OSI/TCP-IP layers, LAN/WAN, wireless, routers, switches, firewalls.
Cloud and virtualisation change who operates which component (shared responsibility).
Hardware maintenance, monitoring and capacity reports support reliability.

terms.d: Seven-layer reference model: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application.

auditor: Understand the components in scope before testing controls over them.
traps: Fibre optic is the most secure cable type against tapping.

subs.title: Networking
points: OSI/TCP-IP models, LAN/WAN technologies, devices and topologies.
LAN topologies: star, bus, ring, mesh; switches segment collision domains, routers separate broadcast domains.
WAN options: leased lines, MPLS, SD-WAN, VPN over internet; each trades cost, performance and security.
Auditors check network diagrams are current, devices are hardened and changes are controlled.
subs.tip: Fibre is hardest to tap; wireless is easiest to intercept.

subs.title: Computer Hardware Components and Architectures
points: Processors, memory, storage, input/output; server and client architectures.
Components: CPU, memory, storage, input/output, buses; architectures include client-server and multi-tier.
Risks: hardware failure, obsolescence, insufficient capacity.

subs.title: Common Enterprise Back-End Devices
points: Print servers, file servers, application, web, database and proxy servers, appliances.
Back-end devices include file, print, application, web, database and proxy servers and appliances.
Each needs hardening, patching, access control and monitoring appropriate to its role.

subs.title: USB Mass Storage Devices
points: Risks: data leakage, malware, theft; controls: encryption, port control, policy.
USB storage can leak data and introduce malware.
Controls: device control software, encryption of approved devices, blocking autorun, user policy and awareness.
subs.tip: Best control for USB data leakage: approved encrypted devices plus endpoint port control.

subs.title: Wireless Communication Technologies
points: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, RFID, NFC: convenience with interception risks.
Bluetooth, RFID and NFC enable short-range communication but can be intercepted or cloned.
Controls: disable when not needed, pair securely, encrypt, monitor rogue devices.

subs.title: Hardware Maintenance Program
points: Planned preventive maintenance, vendor contracts and logs.
Preventive maintenance reduces unplanned outages.
Maintenance logs, vendor contracts and schedules should be reviewed by the auditor.

subs.title: Hardware Reviews
points: Check capacity, utilisation, maintenance and replacement plans.
Review acquisition plans, capacity utilisation, maintenance records and replacement planning.
Check hardware is under support or has a risk-accepted plan.

sections.title: IT Asset Management
sections.summary: Covers knowing and managing every IT asset across its lifecycle.
points: Maintain a complete inventory of hardware, software and licences with owners.
Lifecycle: plan, acquire, deploy, maintain, retire, dispose securely.
Asset data feeds patching, risk assessment, licence compliance and incident response.

terms.d: Configuration management database: records configuration items and relationships.

auditor: Reconcile the inventory to network discovery results.
traps: Unknown assets cannot be secured or patched.

sections.title: Job Scheduling and Production Process Automation
sections.summary: Explains controlled, automated running of production jobs.
points: Scheduling tools run jobs in sequence with dependencies and restart points.
Changes to schedules follow change management; job logs and exceptions are reviewed.
Automation reduces manual error and improves reliability.

terms.d: Software that automatically runs production jobs on a defined schedule.

auditor: Check who can change job definitions and how failed jobs are handled.
traps: Unauthorized changes to job schedules can bypass program change controls.

subs.title: Job Scheduling Software
points: Automates job runs; reduces operator error; needs restricted access to schedules.
Scheduling software runs jobs automatically with dependencies, priorities and restart points.
Benefits: fewer manual errors, consistent processing, audit trail of job runs.

subs.title: Scheduling Reviews
points: Review schedule changes, exceptions and reruns.
Review who can change schedules, how changes are approved and how abnormal ends are handled.
Compare job logs to the approved schedule.

sections.title: System Interfaces
sections.summary: Covers controls over data exchanged between systems.
points: Interfaces include file transfers, APIs, messaging and middleware.
Controls: inventory of interfaces with owners, reconciliation of counts and totals, error handling, encryption in transit, authentication.
Interface failures can silently corrupt or lose data.

terms.d: Application programming interface used for system-to-system communication.

auditor: Test reconciliations between source and target systems.
traps: Undocumented interfaces are a common source of unmanaged risk.

subs.title: Risk Associated With System Interfaces
points: Data loss, duplication, corruption, unauthorised access and unclear ownership.
Risks: data loss or duplication, corruption, unauthorised access in transit, unclear ownership, failures not noticed.

subs.title: Controls Associated With System Interfaces
points: Inventory, ownership, reconciliation, encryption, error handling, monitoring.
Maintain an interface inventory with owners and data flows.
Reconcile counts and totals, encrypt sensitive transfers, alert on failures and test interfaces after changes.
subs.tip: Reconciliation is the key detective control for interfaces.

sections.title: End-User Computing and Shadow IT
sections.summary: Explains risks of user-developed tools and unapproved technology and how to control them.
points: End-user computing (spreadsheets, macros, small databases) can support critical decisions without IT controls.
Shadow IT: technology used without IT/security approval (often cloud SaaS).
Risks: data leakage, unpatched vulnerabilities, no backup, inaccurate results, compliance breaches.
Controls: policy and approval process, inventory of critical EUCs, IT as a service partner, procurement review, restricted admin rights, user education, monitoring (e.g. CASB).

terms.d: Systems or services used without the approval of IT or security.
End-user computing: applications built and run by business users.

auditor: Identify critical EUC tools and test their change, access and backup controls.
traps: Banning tools alone rarely works; providing approved alternatives is the better answer.

subs.title: End-User Computing
points: User-built tools (spreadsheets, databases) used for business decisions.
Risks: errors, no change control, no backup; controls: inventory, testing, access, versioning.
EUC is flexible but often lacks testing, version control, backup and access restriction.
Critical EUCs should be inventoried, risk-rated and brought under proportionate controls.

subs.title: Shadow IT
points: Technology used without IT approval; controls: policy, procurement review, consolidation, restricted rights, education, monitoring.
Shadow IT grows when official IT is slow or unaware of business needs.
Discovery tools (e.g. CASB, network monitoring) help find unapproved services.
subs.tip: Best fix: approved alternatives plus policy, not only prohibition.

sections.title: Systems Availability and Capacity Management
sections.summary: Covers keeping services available and planning capacity for demand.
points: Availability management uses redundancy, clustering, load balancing and monitoring.
Capacity planning forecasts demand for processing, storage and network resources.
Performance reports and trend analysis prevent outages.

terms.d: Ensuring IT capacity meets current and future business needs cost-effectively.

auditor: Check capacity plans exist and are based on business forecasts.
traps: Reactive capacity upgrades indicate weak planning.

subs.title: IS Architecture and Software
points: How systems, software and infrastructure fit together to deliver services.
IS architecture connects hardware, system software, applications and networks to deliver services.

subs.title: Operating Systems
points: Manage hardware and resources; secure configuration and patching are key.
OS manages processes, memory, files and devices; configuration determines security.
Controls: hardened builds, patching, restricted admin rights, logging of privileged activity.

subs.title: Access Control Software
points: Controls who can access system resources; logs violations.
Access control software enforces identification, authentication and authorisation for system resources.
Violation logs must be reviewed.

subs.title: Data Communications Software
points: Manages data transfer between systems; needs integrity and security controls.
Communications software controls data transfer; ensure integrity checks and encryption.

subs.title: Utility Programs
points: Powerful tools that can bypass controls; restrict and log their use.
Utilities (e.g. disk editors, database tools) can change data directly and bypass application controls.
Restrict to authorised staff, log usage, remove from production where possible.
subs.tip: Unrestricted utility programs can alter data without audit trails.

subs.title: Software Licensing Issues
points: Track licences to avoid legal and financial penalties; use inventory and metering.
Unlicensed software creates legal and financial exposure.
Controls: central purchasing, licence inventory, metering software, periodic audits.

subs.title: Source Code Management
points: Version control, access restrictions, code review, escrow for vendor code.
Source code repositories need access control, version history and protection from tampering.
Escrow agreements protect against vendor failure.

subs.title: Capacity Management
points: Monitor utilisation and plan resources ahead of demand.
Capacity management monitors CPU, memory, storage and network trends to forecast needs.

sections.title: Problem and Incident Management
sections.summary: Distinguishes restoring service quickly (incident) from removing root causes (problem).
points: Incident management: log, classify, prioritise, resolve or escalate, close.
Problem management: root cause analysis, known error records, permanent fixes.
Help desk metrics and trend analysis identify recurring problems.

terms.d: A problem with a documented root cause and workaround.

auditor: Check incidents are logged completely and recurring incidents trigger problem records.
traps: Root cause = problem management, not incident management.

subs.title: Problem Management
points: Find and remove root causes of incidents.
Problem management performs root cause analysis and records known errors with workarounds.
Proactive problem management uses trends to prevent incidents.

subs.title: Process of Incident Handling
points: Detect, log, classify, prioritise, resolve, close; escalate when needed.
Incidents are detected, logged, classified, prioritised, investigated, resolved and closed.
Escalation rules ensure major incidents reach the right people quickly.

subs.title: Detection, Documentation, Control, Resolution and Reporting of Abnormal Conditions
points: Abnormal conditions are logged and investigated; trends reported to management.
Abnormal conditions (e.g. abends, errors) must be logged, investigated and resolved with management reporting.

subs.title: Support/Help Desk
points: First point of contact; logs, prioritises and tracks issues.
The help desk records every request, gives first-line resolution and escalates complex issues.
Ticket data supports trend analysis and service improvement.

subs.title: Network Management Tools
points: Response time reports, downtime reports, protocol analysers, SNMP monitoring.
Tools: response time reports, downtime reports, help desk reports, protocol analysers, SNMP-based monitors.

subs.title: Problem Management Reporting Reviews
points: Check that problems are logged, analysed and closed on time.
Review whether problems are recorded, analysed, resolved on time and reported.

sections.title: IT Change, Configuration and Patch Management
sections.summary: Explains controlling changes to production systems, configurations and patches.
points: Change process: request, assess impact, approve (e.g. CAB), test, implement, review.
Emergency changes are documented and approved retrospectively.
Patch management: inventory, prioritise by risk, test, deploy, verify.
Segregate development, test and production environments.

terms.d: Change advisory board that assesses and approves changes.

auditor: Sample production changes and trace them back to approvals and tests.
traps: Programmers should not have access to production.

subs.title: Patch Management
points: Inventory, prioritise by risk, test, deploy, verify.
Patch process: identify, assess risk, test, approve, deploy, verify.
Emergency patches follow an expedited but documented route.
subs.tip: Unpatched critical vulnerabilities are a high-risk finding.

subs.title: Release Management
points: Plan and control bundles of changes into production.
Releases bundle changes; plans include testing, approval, deployment and back-out steps.
Major, minor and emergency releases have different approval paths.

subs.title: IS Operations
points: Day-to-day running: monitoring, job control, backups, operator procedures.
IS operations include job processing, monitoring, console control, media management and operator procedures.
Operators should not have programming access to production code.

sections.title: Operational Log Management
sections.summary: New section in the 28th edition: managing operational logs (audit trails) so events can be monitored, investigated and attributed.
points: Logs record type, time, location, source, outcome and identity of parties for each event.
Log types: event, server, system, access, change, availability, threat, database, error and firewall logs.
Log management cycle: collect, generate alerts, store centrally (log server/SIEM), analyse, report concerns, implement action plans.
Secure logs against tampering; centralise them; synchronise time; define retention.
Log review can be a compensating control where segregation of duties is limited.

terms.d: Security information and event management: collects, correlates and alerts on log data.
Chronological record of activities that allows reconstruction of events.

auditor: Check which events are logged, who can alter logs, and whether alerts are reviewed and acted on.
traps: Logs kept on the same server administrators control are not reliable evidence.

subs.title: Types of Logs
points: Event, server, system, access, change, availability, threat, database, error, firewall logs.
Event log: logins, failed passwords, application events.
Server and system logs: restarts, updates, OS errors and warnings.
Access, change, availability, threat, database, error and firewall logs serve different monitoring needs.
subs.tip: Availability logs evidence SLA uptime; access logs show who used sensitive data.

subs.title: Log Management
points: Collect, alert, store centrally, analyse, report, act; protect logs from tampering.
Cycle: collect data, generate alerts, store logs, analyse data, report concerns, implement action plans.
Infrastructure: log generation (hosts), analysis and storage (log servers), monitoring (e.g. SIEM rules and thresholds).
Protect logs from alteration; centralise them; define retention.
subs.tip: Logs are only useful if someone reviews and acts on them.

sections.title: IT Service Level Management
sections.summary: Covers defining, agreeing and monitoring service levels.
points: SLAs with the business; OLAs between internal teams; underpinning contracts with vendors.
Service catalogue defines services, owners and targets.
Reports must be based on independently measured data.

terms.d: Operational level agreement between internal IT groups supporting an SLA.

auditor: Recalculate SLA metrics from source logs.
traps: Provider self-reported SLA data needs verification.

subs.title: Service Level Agreements
points: Define services, targets, measures and responsibilities.
SLAs define services, measures, targets, responsibilities, reporting and penalties.
OLAs and underpinning contracts support the SLA.

subs.title: Monitoring of Service Levels
points: Measure actual performance against SLAs using objective data.
Service levels are monitored with objective data and reviewed regularly with the business.

subs.title: Service Levels and Enterprise Architecture
points: Architecture decisions must support required service levels.
Architecture choices (redundancy, capacity) must support agreed service levels.

sections.title: Database Management
sections.summary: Explains DBMS architecture, models and controls.
points: DBMS architecture and data dictionary/directory; metadata types.
Models: hierarchical, network, relational, object, NoSQL; normalisation reduces redundancy.
Controls: restricted direct access, DBA activity logging and review, backup/recovery, integrity constraints, encryption.

terms.d: Organising tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies.
Foreign keys always refer to existing primary keys.

auditor: Review privileged database accounts and how DBA actions are monitored.
traps: The DBA should not review their own activity.

subs.title: DBMS Architecture
points: Schemas, data dictionary/directory and metadata.
Three-schema view: external (user views), conceptual (logical model) and internal (physical storage).
Data dictionary/directory holds metadata about data definitions and usage.

subs.title: Database Structure
points: Hierarchical, network, relational, object and NoSQL models.
Hierarchical, network, relational and object-oriented models; NoSQL for flexible or large-scale data.
Normalisation reduces redundancy and update anomalies.

subs.title: Database Controls
points: Access restrictions, integrity constraints, logging, backup, DBA monitoring.
Controls: access through approved interfaces only, integrity constraints, concurrency control, backup and recovery, audit logging.
DBA activity should be logged and independently reviewed.

subs.title: Database Reviews
points: Review design, access, interfaces, backup and performance.
Review design, access controls, interfaces, backup and recovery, performance and DBA procedures.

sections.title: Business Impact Analysis
sections.summary: Identifies critical processes and the impact of disruption to set recovery priorities.
points: BIA determines criticality, impact over time, dependencies, RTO and RPO.
Inputs from business process owners through interviews, questionnaires and workshops.
Results drive classification (critical, vital, sensitive, non-critical) and recovery strategy.

terms.d: Maximum tolerable downtime before the business suffers unacceptable harm.

auditor: Check BIA is current and approved by business owners.
traps: BIA comes before choosing recovery strategies.

subs.title: Classification of Operations and Criticality Analysis
points: Rank systems as critical, vital, sensitive, non-critical based on impact.
Critical: cannot be performed manually; very low tolerance to interruption.
Vital: can be done manually for a short time.
Sensitive: manual for a tolerable period at extra cost. Non-critical: can be interrupted for long periods.

sections.title: System and Operational Resilience
sections.summary: Covers designing systems to withstand and recover from disruption.
points: Resilience techniques: redundancy, fault tolerance, clustering, RAID, geographically dispersed sites.
RTO drives recovery speed; RPO drives data replication or backup frequency.
Lower RTO/RPO costs more; decisions balance cost against impact.

terms.d: Recovery time objective: maximum acceptable downtime.
Recovery point objective: maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.

auditor: Check resilience designs meet BIA requirements.
traps: Low RPO needs frequent backups or mirroring; low RTO needs hot sites or high availability.

subs.title: Application Resiliency and Disaster Recovery Methods
points: Clustering, load balancing, failover.
Clustering (active-active or active-passive), load balancing and failover improve application resilience.

subs.title: Telecommunication Networks Resiliency and Disaster Recovery Methods
points: Redundancy, alternative routing, diverse routing, last-mile protection, voice recovery.
Redundancy, alternative routing, diverse routing, long-haul diversity, last-mile protection and voice recovery protect communications.

sections.title: Data Backup, Storage and Restoration
sections.summary: Explains backup schemes, media, offsite storage and restore testing.
points: Full, incremental and differential backups; rotation schemes such as grandfather-father-son.
Backups stored offsite or in separate cloud regions; protected and encrypted.
Restores must be tested regularly; immutable backups help against ransomware.

terms.d: Copies all changes since the last full backup.
Copies changes since the last backup of any type.

auditor: Review restore test results, not just backup job success.
traps: Untested backups give no assurance of recovery.

subs.title: Data Storage Resiliency and Disaster Recovery Methods
points: RAID levels, replication, mirroring.
RAID protects against disk failure; replication and mirroring copy data to another location.
Synchronous replication gives near-zero RPO but needs short distance.

subs.title: Backup and Restoration
points: Offsite storage, media handling, cloud backup, restore testing.
Backups need offsite or separate-region copies, media protection, encryption and regular restore tests.

subs.title: Backup Schemes
points: Full, incremental, differential; rotation (e.g. grandfather-father-son).
Full: all data. Incremental: changes since last backup of any type. Differential: changes since last full.
Rotation schemes such as grandfather-father-son balance retention and media use.
subs.tip: Fastest restore: full + differential; smallest daily backup: incremental.

sections.title: Business Continuity Plan
sections.summary: Covers developing, testing and maintaining the BCP.
points: BCP lifecycle: policy, BIA, strategy, plan, training, testing, maintenance.
Plan content: roles, invocation criteria, communication, recovery procedures, contact lists.
Tests: checklist, walk-through/table-top, simulation, parallel, full interruption.
Senior management approves the plan; it must be reviewed after changes and tests.

terms.d: Discussion-based walk-through of a scenario by the response team.

auditor: Check test results against objectives and that gaps are corrected.
traps: Full interruption tests are the most disruptive and least frequent.

subs.title: IT Business Continuity Planning
points: IT continuity supports the overall BCP.
IT continuity ensures systems supporting critical processes can recover within required times.

subs.title: Disasters and Other Disruptive Events
points: Natural, technical and human-caused events, including pandemics and cyberattacks.
Events include natural disasters, technical failures, cyberattacks, pandemics and supplier failure.

subs.title: Business Continuity Planning Process
points: Policy, BIA, strategy, plan, training, testing, maintenance.
Steps: policy, BIA, strategy, plan development, training/awareness, testing, maintenance.

subs.title: Business Continuity Policy
points: Management’s statement of intent and scope for continuity.
The policy, approved by senior management, states scope, objectives and responsibilities.

subs.title: Business Continuity Planning Incident Management
points: Classify incidents by severity to decide when to invoke the plan.
Incidents are classified (e.g. negligible, minor, major, crisis) to decide when to invoke plans.

subs.title: Development of Business Continuity Plans
points: Based on BIA results and chosen strategies.
Plans are built from the BIA and chosen recovery strategies; owners keep them current.

subs.title: Other Issues in Plan Development
points: Involve all functions, consider dependencies, staff safety, communications.
Consider staff safety, dependencies on suppliers, communications and insurance.

subs.title: Components of a Business Continuity Plan
points: Roles, teams, contacts, procedures, resources, insurance, communications.
Components: roles and teams, contact lists, recovery procedures, resources, alternative sites, communications, insurance.

subs.title: Plan Testing
points: Desk-based, walk-through, preparedness, full operational tests.
Test types: checklist, walk-through, simulation, parallel, full interruption.
Each test has objectives, measured results and corrective actions.

subs.title: Business Continuity Management Good Practices
points: Continuous review, training, testing and improvement.
Good practices: regular review, training, testing, integration with change management.

subs.title: Auditing Business Continuity
points: Review plan currency, test results, BIA, offsite storage and team readiness.
Auditor reviews plan currency, BIA, test results, offsite storage, contracts and team readiness.
subs.tip: An untested plan gives little assurance.

sections.title: Disaster Recovery Plans
sections.summary: Explains recovering IT services after a disaster.
points: Recovery sites: hot, warm, cold, mirrored, mobile, cloud-based, reciprocal agreements.
DRP teams have clear roles; plans are tested and updated.
Recovery strategy is chosen to meet RTO/RPO at acceptable cost.

terms.d: Fully equipped site ready to run within hours.

auditor: Check DR test scope, results and updates to the plan.
traps: Reciprocal agreements are the least reliable recovery option.

subs.title: RPO, RTO and Mean Time to Repair
points: RPO limits data loss; RTO limits downtime; MTTR measures repair speed.
RPO: maximum data loss in time; drives backup frequency.
RTO: maximum downtime; drives recovery strategy.
MTTR: average time to repair; lower means faster recovery.

subs.title: Recovery Strategies
points: Choose based on criticality, cost and RTO/RPO.
Strategy depends on criticality, RTO/RPO, cost and risk; lower targets cost more.

subs.title: Recovery Alternatives
points: Hot, warm, cold, mobile, mirrored sites; reciprocal agreements; cloud DR.
Hot site: ready in hours. Warm: partly equipped. Cold: space only. Mirrored: duplicate running site.
Mobile sites, reciprocal agreements and cloud DR are further options.
subs.tip: Reciprocal agreements are the least reliable alternative.

subs.title: Development of Disaster Recovery Plans
points: Document procedures, teams and responsibilities.
DRP documents recovery procedures, teams, responsibilities and resources for IT.

subs.title: Disaster Recovery Testing Methods
points: Checklist, walk-through, simulation, parallel, full interruption.
Tests range from checklist reviews to full interruption; results update the plan.

subs.title: Invoking Disaster Recovery Plans
points: Clear criteria and authority for declaring a disaster.
Define who can declare a disaster and the criteria for invoking the DRP.

sections.title: Information Asset Security Policies, Frameworks, Standards and Guidelines
sections.summary: Covers the security policy framework, ISMS and the roles that govern information security.
points: Security policy approved by senior management sets direction; supported by standards and procedures.
Frameworks: ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS, ISO/IEC 27002 controls, NIST CSF.
Roles: board, executive management, CISO, data owners, custodians, users, auditors.

terms.d: Information security management system: a managed, continually improving approach to security.

auditor: Check policy approval, communication and periodic review.
traps: Senior management commitment is the most critical success factor.

subs.title: Information Asset Security Policies, Procedures and Guidelines
points: Approved security policy supported by standards, procedures and guidelines.
Policies are approved by senior management, communicated, acknowledged and reviewed regularly.
Procedures and guidelines translate policy into practice.

subs.title: Information Security Frameworks and Standards
points: ISO/IEC 27001/27002, NIST CSF, CIS Controls.
ISO/IEC 27001 (ISMS requirements), 27002 (control guidance), NIST CSF (identify, protect, detect, respond, recover).

subs.title: Information Security Baselines
points: Minimum security configurations for systems; deviations approved.
Baselines are minimum configurations per platform; deviations need approval.
Compliance is checked with configuration scanning.

sections.title: Physical and Environmental Controls
sections.summary: Explains protecting facilities and equipment from physical and environmental threats.
points: Physical access: badges, biometrics, mantraps, guards, CCTV, visitor logs.
Environmental: UPS, generators, fire detection and suppression, water detection, HVAC, raised floors.
Power issues: blackout, brownout, sag, spike, surge, EMI.

terms.d: Two-door entry where only one door opens at a time, preventing tailgating.

auditor: Inspect facilities and test that alarms and suppression systems are maintained.
traps: Dry-pipe systems reduce accidental water damage; halon is no longer used.

subs.title: Environmental Exposures and Controls
points: Power issues, fire, water, temperature; UPS, generators, suppression systems, detectors.
Power: blackout, brownout, sag, spike, surge, EMI; controls include UPS, generators, surge protection.
Fire: detectors, alarms, suppression (pre-action/dry-pipe, clean agents); water detectors; HVAC.
subs.tip: Halon is banned; dry-pipe systems reduce accidental water damage.

subs.title: Physical Access Exposures and Controls
points: Badges, biometrics, mantraps, guards, CCTV, visitor logs.
Controls: badges, biometrics, mantraps, guards, CCTV, visitor logs and escorts, low-profile locations.
Review access lists and logs regularly.

subs.title: Industrial Control Systems Security
points: SCADA/OT systems need segmentation, restricted access and careful patching.
ICS/SCADA controls physical processes; availability and safety come first.
Segment from IT networks, restrict remote access, patch carefully.

sections.title: Identity and Access Management
sections.summary: Covers identification, authentication, authorisation and managing access through its lifecycle.
points: Least privilege, need to know and segregation of duties guide access design.
Authentication factors: know, have, are; MFA combines different types.
Access models: DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC; SSO and federation need strong authentication.
Lifecycle: request, approve (by owner), provision, review periodically, revoke promptly.
Biometrics: FAR (security risk), FRR (inconvenience), EER for comparison.

terms.d: Giving users only the access required for their role.
False acceptance rate: impostors accepted.

auditor: Test joiner/mover/leaver processes and periodic access reviews.
traps: Two passwords is not MFA.
Data owners approve access, not IT administrators.

subs.title: Identity and Access Management
points: Manage identities and access across their lifecycle.
IAM covers identification, authentication, authorisation, provisioning and deprovisioning.

subs.title: Authentication, Authorization and Accounting
points: AAA: verify identity, grant rights, record actions.
Authentication proves identity; authorisation grants rights; accounting logs actions.

subs.title: Zero-Trust Architecture
points: Never trust, always verify; continuous verification and least privilege.
Zero trust: verify explicitly, use least privilege, assume breach; access decided per request.

subs.title: Privileged Access Management
points: Vaulting, just-in-time access, session recording for admins.
PAM vaults privileged credentials, grants just-in-time access and records sessions.
subs.tip: Privileged accounts are the highest-value targets.

subs.title: Directory Services
